walls.name: Archaic wall of the Palatine (Carandini's 'Romulean' wall)

phases.t: First wall on the north slope (c. 730-720 BC): cappellaccio footings with a timber and clay superstructure, found by Carandini's excavations between the Arch of Titus and the House of the Vestals.
Rebuilt (second phase, c. 675 BC).
Third phase (c. 600 BC).
Fourth phase (c. 530 BC); aristocratic houses then line the Sacra Via against it.
No longer maintained; built over by the houses of the north slope. End date is a guess.

walls.note: Only the north-slope stretch (c. 80 m, around [12.4870, 41.8910]) has been excavated; the full circuit around the foot of the hill is Carandini's hypothesis, partly modelled on the Palatine pomerium of Tacitus (Ann. 12.24) and drawn here a few metres inside the modern streets at the base (Via di S. Teodoro, Via dei Cerchi, Via di S. Gregorio). Its dating and even its function as a wall (rather than a pomerial boundary) are disputed.
scholarship: Carandini and Carafa (eds.), The Atlas of Ancient Rome (2017) I, Palatine

walls.name: Fortifications of the Capitol and the Arx

phases.t: Cappellaccio walls round the cliff edges of the Capitolium and Arx (remains below the retaining wall above Vicolo della Rupe Tarpea and near the Aracoeli stairs).
The Capitol alone holds out against the Gauls; Manlius repulses the night assault on the Arx (Livy 5.47).
West side rebuilt as part of the Servian circuit in Grotta Oscura tufa.
South-east side masked by the substructures of the Tabularium and the Area Capitolina; the walls survive as retaining walls.

walls.note: Drawn along the cliff edges of the two summits joined by the Asylum saddle. The western half coincides with the Servian line. East side (towards the Forum) conjectural; no city gate except the clivus entrances (Porta Pandana) is recorded.
scholarship: Platner-Ashby 351 (remains on the north side of the Capitol)

walls.name: Archaic ('Servian') circuit in cappellaccio

phases.t: Tradition credits Servius Tullius (Livy 1.44.3; Dionysius 4.13): cappellaccio blocks (0.20-0.30 x 0.55-0.66 x 0.75-0.90 m) with an earth agger on the Esquiline plateau.
Gallic sack: the circuit fails to stop the Senones (Livy 5.38-41).
Replacement in Grotta Oscura tufa begins; old stretches incorporated or dismantled.

walls.note: Whether a complete 6th-century circuit existed is debated (Cifani; Fontaine vs. those who see only an agger and hilltop defences). Drawn on the same course as the 4th-century wall, which reused it in places (cappellaccio stretches survive at the agger and on the Aventine).

walls.name: Servian Wall (Republican circuit)

sections.name: Quirinal saddle (cut away for the Forum of Trajan)
Forum Boarium / riverside section between Porta Trigemina and Porta Carmentalis

dims.blocks: Grotta Oscura tufa, alternate headers and stretchers, courses 0.58-0.61 m high, Greek-looking mason's marks

phases.t: Censors let the contract for a wall of squared stone (Livy 6.32.1); work in 30-40 m lots by separate gangs, possibly with Syracusan masons; Grotta Oscura tufa from the territory of conquered Veii.
Wall and towers repaired / completed (Livy 7.20.9). Height about 10 m, thickness about 4 m; agger and ditch across the Esquiline plateau.
After Trasimene the walls and towers are repaired (Livy 22.8.6).
Further repairs during the Hannibalic War; in 211 Hannibal rides up to the Porta Collina (Livy 26.10).

Bellum Octavianum: the circuit is refurbished for artillery, with arched catapult embrasures (viale Aventino stretch; the Palazzo Antonelli arch on the Quirinal is attributed to this work) (Appian, BC 1.66-69).
Battle of the Colline Gate (Sulla against the Samnites) outside the north-east corner.

No longer maintained under Augustus; houses press against both faces and the circuit becomes hard to trace (Dionysius 4.13.5); Maecenas lays gardens over the agger and Esquiline cemetery (Horace, Sat. 1.8.14-16).
The stretch across the Quirinal saddle disappears in the cutting for Trajan's Forum and Markets.
Stands only in fragments embedded in houses, horti and public buildings; gates survive as arches (Porta Esquilina rebuilt as the Arch of Gallienus in 262).
Remnants used as quarry and foundations; long stretches still visible on the agger and Aventine.

walls.note: Course drawn through the surviving stretches and gate sites: Aracoeli and Capitoline foot, Largo Magnanapoli, Palazzo Colonna, Via della Dataria, Via delle Scuderie and Via dei Giardini, Largo S. Susanna, Via Salandra, Via Goito / Via XX Settembre (Porta Collina), the agger remains north of and in front of Termini and in the station, Piazza Manfredo Fanti, the Arch of Gallienus, Via Mecenate (Auditorium of Maecenas), Via Poliziano, S. Clemente, the Arch of Dolabella, Porta Capena, S. Balbina, viale Aventino / Piazza Albania, Via di Sant'Anselmo and the west cliff of the Aventine (S. Sabina). Between surviving pieces the line follows the hill edges; my trace measures about 8.3 km against the c. 11 km usually quoted, because real wall lines zig-zag along contours. The river section is unknown (Livy suggests the wall ran down from the Aventine to the Tiber leaving the port open).
scholarship: Säflund, Le mura di Roma repubblicana (1932)

walls.name: Agger and fossa of the Servian Wall (Esquiline plateau)

phases.t: Front wall of Grotta Oscura blocks 4 m thick backed by an earth rampart about 30 m wide (Dionysius: 7 stadia long, 50 ft thick) and fronted by a ditch about 100 Roman feet (30-36 m) wide and 30 ft (9 m) deep. Porta Viminalis the only gate between the Collina and Esquilina.
The rampart becomes a promenade ('aggere in aprico spatiari', Horace Sat. 1.8.15); the ditch beyond is filled with the Esquiline dumps and gardens.
Rampart still visible; the ditch is built over.

walls.note: Line from the Porta Collina (Via XX Settembre / Via Goito) to the Porta Esquilina (Arch of Gallienus). Rampart on the inner (west) side; ditch line offset 24 m outward (east) to its centre. Large stretches seen in the 1860s-1870s works for Termini and the Esquiline quarter; the 94 m stretch in Piazza dei Cinquecento stands to about 8 m.
scholarship: Lanciani, Ruins and Excavations of Ancient Rome (1897) 67-71

walls.name: Aurelian Wall (left bank: Campus Martius river wall and land circuit)

sections.name: River wall along the Campus Martius from Ponte Sisto to Ponte Regina Margherita and across to the Porta Flaminia (demolished; traced on the Lungotevere)

Land circuit, Porta Flaminia to the Tiber at Testaccio (traced from the surviving remains as mapped in OpenStreetMap; demolished gaps at the Porta Salaria / Porta Pia area and at Porta Ostiensis - Pyramid bridged straight)
Outer (north and east) walls of the Castra Praetoria, raised and incorporated
River wall at Testaccio, about 800 m north along the left bank (vanished; a medieval chain tower survives on Lungotevere Testaccio)

phases.t: Aurelian orders the circuit after the Juthungian invasion of Italy; built fast by the city's collegia, incorporating existing structures (Castra Praetoria, Pyramid of Cestius, Amphitheatrum Castrense, aqueduct arches, the Horti walls of the Muro Torto, tombs and insulae).
Largely complete at Aurelian's death. Curtain about 6-8 m high over 2 m footings, 3.3-3.5 m thick, with a crenellated walkway; square towers every 100 Roman feet with a ballista chamber.
Finished under Probus (Zosimus 1.49).

Maxentius begins a refurbishment against Constantine: a ditch (fossa) is dug, some stretches and the Castra Praetoria walls are raised; the attribution of the upper gallery to Maxentius (Richmond) is now doubted.
Constantine disbands the praetorians and razes the camp walls facing the city; the outer camp walls stay in the circuit.

Honorius and Stilicho double the height (to roughly 15-16 m): a covered gallery with arrow slits is built on the old walkway and a new open, crenellated walkway on top; towers raised by a storey; most gates rebuilt in travertine, many reduced to one arch; dedicatory inscriptions of 401-402 at the Tiburtina, Praenestina-Labicana and Portuensis (CIL VI 1188-1190).
Works completed for Honorius' triumph of 403; the Mausoleum of Hadrian is turned into a bridgehead fortress.
24 August: Alaric's Goths enter by the Porta Salaria; the wall itself is not breached.
Mid-5th-century repairs under Valentinian III after earthquake damage (date and extent uncertain).
Vandal sack: Geiseric enters without siege.
Theoderic funds restorations (Cassiodorus, Variae 1.25, 2.34; brick stamps REGE THEODERICO).
Belisarius repairs the circuit, recuts the ditch and fits merlons with a lateral wing (Procopius 5.14.15); the Muro Torto is left as it was.
Siege by Witiges (March 537 - March 538): assaults at the Porta Salaria, Praenestina (Vivarium), Aurelia/Mausoleum and Flaminia; the Goths cut the aqueducts.
17 December: Totila enters through the Porta Asinaria (Isaurian guards' treachery) and pulls down about a third of the circuit (Procopius 7.22.6-7).
Spring: Belisarius reoccupies Rome and closes the breaches in 25 days with rubble laid dry or in clay, without new gates (Procopius 7.24.3-6).
Totila retakes Rome (the Isaurians open the Porta Ostiensis, January 550 in some reckonings) and restores the circuit to hold it (Procopius 7.36-37).
Narses takes the city after Busta Gallorum; the circuit stays in use, as rebuilt.

walls.note: Land circuit chained from the OpenStreetMap 'Mura Aureliane' relation (surviving stretches, simplified to about 3.5 m), from the Porta del Popolo clockwise past the Muro Torto (a retaining wall of the Horti Aciliorum/Pinciani reused), Porta Pinciana, Salaria, Nomentana, the Castra Praetoria salient, Porta Chiusa, Tiburtina, the Porta Maggiore aqueduct arches, the Amphitheatrum Castrense, Porta Asinaria, Metronia, Latina, Appia, Ardeatina, Ostiensis and the Pyramid, to the Tiber at Testaccio. The river walls are reconstructed on the Lungotevere roads, roughly on the old bank. The line is open: the river between Ponte Sisto and Testaccio was covered by the Trastevere salient (see aurelian_wall_trastevere). Lengths: about 16.7 km here plus 2.2 km in Trastevere, against the 19 km usually given.
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Dey, The Aurelian Wall and the Refashioning of Imperial Rome, AD 271-855 (2011)

walls.name: Aurelian Wall (Trastevere salient)

sections.name: Porta Portuensis - Porta Aurelia - Porta Septimiana; demolished by Urban VIII (1640s) except the stretch at Porta Settimiana

walls.note: From the right bank at the Porta Portuensis (start of Via Portuense at Via E. Bezzi, about 450 m south of the later Porta Portese) along Via degli Orti di Trastevere and Piazza B. da Feltre, up Viale Glorioso and Via A. Masina to the Porta Aurelia (Porta S. Pancrazio) on the Janiculum summit, then down along Via di Porta S. Pancrazio and the surviving stretch through the Porta Settimiana to the river just north of Ponte Sisto. Course per it.wikipedia 'Mura aureliane' and Richmond; the surviving stretch at Porta Settimiana is from OpenStreetMap.
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930)
Dey, The Aurelian Wall and the Refashioning of Imperial Rome, AD 271-855 (2011)

walls.name: Bridgehead fortification of the Mausoleum of Hadrian

phases.t: Honorius turns the mausoleum into a fortress covering the Pons Aelius, its precinct wall rebuilt with corner towers and linked to the Porta Aurelia-Sancti Petri on the left bank (Procopius 5.22.12-13).
The garrison breaks up the statues of the mausoleum and hurls them at the Goths (Procopius 5.22.20-22).

walls.note: Modelled as a 124 m square enclosure around the 89 m drum base, aligned on the Pons Aelius axis (bearing 176). The exact form of the Honorian enclosure is not known; the bridge itself and the mausoleum belong to the buildings collection.
scholarship: Richmond, The City Wall of Imperial Rome (1930) 22-25

walls.name: Castra Praetoria, outer walls (north and east)

phases.t: Sejanus concentrates the praetorian cohorts in a walled camp of about 440 x 380 m with rounded corners (Tacitus, Ann. 4.2; Suetonius, Tib. 37); early brick walls about 4.7 m high with crenellations.
Besieged by the people in the riots against the praetorians (Herodian 7.11-12).
Raised and absorbed into the Aurelian Wall (continued as part of aurelian_wall from 275).

walls.note: Corners from the OpenStreetMap wall trace: NW [12.503919, 41.907879], NE [12.508177, 41.908935], SE [12.509969, 41.905338]. The original crenellations are still visible below the Aurelian raising.

walls.name: Castra Praetoria, inner walls (south and west, facing the city)

phases.t: Built with the camp.
Left standing inside the new circuit.
Razed by Constantine after Milvian Bridge when he disbands the guard (Aurelius Victor, Caes. 40.25; Zosimus 2.17.2).

walls.note: SW corner computed as NW + (SE - NE). Constantine's demolition removed the walls facing the city, leaving the outer ones in the Aurelian circuit.
